docs.title: AI Assistant for Knowledge Workers
docs.text:
An intelligent AI assistant powered by an LLM through the Anthropic Messages API, Skills and MCP (Model Context Protocol) that helps knowledge workers with periodic automated monitoring and interactive querying.

Get Started View on GitHub

docs.title: Why ai-assist?
docs.text:
• 🤖 AI-Powered

    Uses an LLM via the Anthropic Messages API for intelligent analysis, with abstract model tiers (low / medium / high) selectable per task.

  • 🔌 MCP Integration

    Connect to any MCP server — DCI, Jira, GitHub, Google Docs, Second Brain — for tools and live data.

  • 💬 Interactive Mode

    A rich terminal UI with streaming responses, markdown rendering, history search, tab completion, and session model/effort controls.

  • 📊 Monitoring

    Automated scheduled checks with smart desktop, file, and console notifications, plus hot reload.

  • 🧠 Knowledge Graph

    A bi-temporal database with vector embeddings tracking entities, relationships, and conversation memory.

  • 🔄 AWL Workflows

    Script multi-step agent workflows with conditionals, loops, variable propagation, and per-task model/effort controls in the Agent Workflow Language.

  • 🚀 Agent Skills

    Install specialized skills following the agentskills.io specification and run them as /<skill> args.

  • ⚡ Event-Driven Actions

    React to the world with triggers from MQTT, D-Bus, and filesystem changes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# Install uv, then clone and sync
git clone https://github.com/ai-assist-org/ai-assist
cd ai-assist
uv sync

# Configure credentials
cp .env.example .env   # edit with your LLM/MCP credentials

# Run
uv run ai-assist                      # interactive mode (default)
uv run ai-assist /monitor             # monitoring mode
uv run ai-assist /query "..."         # one-off query
uv run ai-assist /run workflow.awl    # execute an AWL workflow

See the Getting Started guide for authentication options and next steps.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: How ai-assist is put together: the query loop, each subsystem's implementation notes, and where things live. User-facing behaviour is documented in README and the guides in this directory; this page is the map for people (and agents) changing the code.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ai-assist CLI                        │
│         (interactive / monitor / query modes)           │
└───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
┌───────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│                    AiAssistAgent                        │
│  - conversation with the model                          │
│  - routes tool calls to MCP servers                     │
│  - multi-turn interactions                              │
└───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        │               │               │
┌───────▼────────┐ ┌────▼───────┐ ┌─────▼──────────┐
│ MCP servers    │ │  internal  │ │   future MCP   │
│ (dci, jira, …) │ │   tools    │ │    servers     │
└────────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘

Five subsystems:

  1. MCP integration (agent.py) — connects to MCP servers and routes tool calls named server_name__tool_name.
  2. AWL runtime (awl_parser.py, awl_runtime.py, awl_ast.py, awl_expressions.py) — the Agent Workflow Language interpreter.
  3. Knowledge graph (knowledge_graph.py) — temporal SQLite database with vector embeddings for entities, change detection and memory.
  4. Agent Skills (skills_loader.py, skills_manager.py) — agentskills.io skills with optional sandboxed scripts.
  5. Event sources (event_sources.py, event_source_mqtt.py, event_source_dbus.py, event_source_file.py) — reactive task triggering.

Interaction modes: interactive (tui_interactive.py), plan mode (plan_mode.py, /plan), monitor (monitors.py, task_runner.py), one-off query (main.py), AWL (awl_runtime.py).

docs.title: MCP agent flow
docs.text:
User → CLI (main.py) → AiAssistAgent (agent.py) → model API
                                ↓
                        MCP server sessions
                        (dci, jira, github, …)
                                ↓
                        tool results → response

Both entry points use the streaming agent loop; query() collects the final answer from query_streaming(), so execution logic lives in the shared streaming path.

  • Time budget: both entry points default to 600 s (AI_ASSIST_QUERY_TIMEOUT); max_time_seconds=NO_TIME_LIMIT (AWL tasks without max_time=, scheduled actions) removes it. Time spent waiting on an approval prompt (pause_timeout()) does not count.
  • Turn budget: soft. At max_turns the model is told to wrap up and gets up to 50% more turns. When that is exhausted, or the time budget passes (checked between turns), the model gets one final turn, offered only internal__finish_task in an AWL task and no tools otherwise.
  • Hard cutoff: a backstop at 1.5× the time budget (_HARD_TIME_LIMIT_FACTOR).
  • Model API failures: query() returns error text unless the caller passes raise_on_api_error=True (AWL tasks and scheduled actions do, also via execute_mcp_prompt), which raises QueryAPIError. raise_on_incomplete=True (AWL tasks) raises QueryIncompleteError when a query stops without a final answer. Both live in query_errors.py.
  • Stream retry: a turn whose stream drops mid-reply (transport/SSL/ connection-reset) is retried up to twice (_STREAM_RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS) without consuming the turn budget, but only if the turn hasn't added to the conversation yet.
  • Context trimming: when messages exceed AI_ASSIST_TOTAL_MESSAGES_PCT of the context window, _trim_oldest_messages drops whole oldest exchanges (the list keeps starting on a user text turn) and never the current query's question or its turns. Each drop is logged.
  • Enclosing queries: an AWL script run from a tool call does not count against the enclosing query (exempt_enclosing_queries_from_timeout()); the script bounds itself per task, and its tasks keep their own budgets.

docs.title: AWL
docs.text:
docs/AWL_SPECIFICATIONS.md is the language reference. Implementation notes that are not in the spec:

  • Task outcome: while a task runs, _build_api_tools offers the agent internal__finish_task (task_result_tool.py). It reports status="success" with the exposed values, or status="failed" with a reason, which fails the task through the normal failure path. A turn that ends without calling it gets one nudge (_finish_nudge_fired); after that, values are extracted from the reply and missing ones stay None — the expose nudge must not guess. Limitation: a nested non-AWL query made during a task also sees the tool.
  • Model tiers: model=low|medium|high|default resolves via resolve_tier (awl_runtime.py) using AI_ASSIST_MODEL_LOW/_MEDIUM/_HIGH, falling back to the session model. default and high fall back to each other. Effort resolves through AiAssistAgent._model_for / _effort_for as effort= override → the model var's :effort suffix → session effort; no sends none.
  • Auto-authorized commands: commands written in backticks are authorized without a prompt only for scripts the user started: /run, an action whose prompt is the script, or — via is_trusted_by_action (awl_executor.py) — a script named by the confirmed prompt of the running action. When such a named script fails or cannot acquire its execution lock, the action is reported as failed even if the agent carries on.
  • Failure propagation: both @start and @goal execution check WorkflowResult.success; a failed cycle cannot complete a goal.
  • Audit attribution: the audit log attributes each tool call to its script and task (AuditLogger.task_context, entered by AWLRuntime).

docs.title: Knowledge graph
docs.text:
Bi-temporal SQLite database tracking entities (DCI jobs, Jira tickets, conversations, knowledge), relationships, valid time (when a fact is true in reality), transaction time (when the agent learned it), and vector embeddings for semantic search (embedding.py, context.py).

  • Temporal tools: kg_snapshot (point-in-time), search_knowledge with since, expire_knowledge.
  • KG synthesis: a nightly task snapshots new/changed reports and discovers connections between entities. It does not extract knowledge from conversations — compaction-time extraction does (below).
  • Compaction-time extraction: in interactive mode, durable facts the user stated are extracted when the conversation is compacted, cleared (/clear), or the session exits (synchronously on exit), as a background task. Extraction reuses an existing project_context key when a new fact is a near-duplicate (semantic similarity ≥ AiAssistAgent.DEDUP_SIM_THRESHOLD), so the KG's last-write-wins upsert supersedes it instead of accreting parallel entries. The threshold is deliberately conservative: a false merge overwrites a distinct fact irrecoverably.
  • Auto context injection: semantically relevant entities are surfaced in the per-query context based on query similarity. Bookkeeping types in KnowledgeGraph.NON_EMBEDDED_TYPES (tool_result, skill_performance) are never embedded, so they stay out of recall.
  • Skill usage: every skill invocation (model-invoked via introspection__get_skill_help, or manual /<skill-name>) is counted as a skill_performance entity (invocation count + last used); /skill/stats shows it. Recording is best-effort and never blocks the run. It is invocation-only (no outcome/confidence) by design; skill_performance.py keeps the confidence machinery for a future outcome-scoring step.

Files: knowledge_graph.py, kg_queries.py, kg_query_tools.py, knowledge_tools.py, embedding.py, context.py.

docs.title: Agent Skills and plugins
docs.text:
Skills follow the agentskills.io spec. Loaded into the system prompt (model-invoked) and user-invocable as /<skill-name> [args]; the SKILL.md body runs as a query with $ARGUMENTS/$1 substitution (quoted segments stay grouped). Opt out with user-invocable: false. Built-in commands take precedence over same-named skills. Implementation: handle_skill_invocation (tui_interactive.py).

Script execution is disabled by default: it requires AI_ASSIST_ALLOW_SCRIPT_EXECUTION=true, runs sandboxed (no API keys, 30 s timeout, 20 KB output limit), and per-skill env vars need an allowlist via /skill/add_env (persisted in ~/.ai-assist/skill_env.json). Files: skills_loader.py, skills_manager.py, script_execution_tools.py, security.py, skill_performance.py.

Plugins load .claude-plugin/plugin.json + skills/*/SKILL.md + legacy commands/*.md + .mcp.json.

  • Plugin skills/commands are registered in the shared skills_manager.loaded_skills dict under namespaced keys (plugin:skill), so every consumer (system prompt, completion, /help, invocation) works unchanged. Namespacing lives at the registry-key layer only, never in SkillMetadata.name.
  • Bundled MCP servers are namespaced (plugin__server) and merged into config.mcp_servers; kept in plugins_manager.plugin_mcp_servers and re-merged after any reload_mcp_servers() / skills reload.
  • agents/ (subagents) and hooks/ are not supported — skipped with a notice.
  • Commands: /plugin/install|uninstall|update|list|search, /plugin/marketplace add [nickname]|update [name]|list. update reinstalls from the recorded source (rollback on failure); marketplace add refuses to mask a different registration and accepts a nickname. A plugin offered by several marketplaces is ambiguous: install errors with the candidates; disambiguate with <name>@<marketplace>. Installing bundled MCP servers prompts before connecting.
  • The agent gets read-only introspection (introspection__list_skills / list_plugins); install/update/uninstall stay human-driven slash commands.

Files: plugins_loader.py, plugins_manager.py, skills_manager.py. User docs: docs/PLUGINS.md.

docs.title: Service management
docs.text:
Cross-platform background service installation for persistent monitoring: systemd user services with journalctl on Linux, launchd user agents with file logging (~/Library/Logs/) on macOS. ServiceBackend is the abstract platform interface; _get_backend() detects the platform. Services preserve the user environment (PATH, env vars) and support multiple instances via config directory naming. File: service.py.

Adding a backend: subclass ServiceBackend in service.py, implement service_file_path, service_content, install, remove, action, status and logs, add platform detection in _get_backend(), and cover it in tests/test_service.py.

docs.title: Sandbox instances
docs.text:
The experimental egress-proxy feature makes the shared Compose bridge internal and drops all capabilities from the agent with no-new-privileges. The generator adds a mitmproxy service on both the internal bridge and a separate upstream network. HTTP clients use CONNECT, with internal MCP and LiteLLM service names in the proxy exclusion list. The CONNECT authority, SNI and HTTP authority must agree. Workloads receive the public CA only. Content rules run in the proxy after the client constructs the HTTP request. For inspected profiles it scans the method, percent-decoded path and query, header names, header values except for Authorization and X-API-Key, and the body. Requests with trailers or unavailable bodies are refused for those profiles. Deployment policies can restrict a destination to a sidecar using required_sources (hostname to service name). Both proxy listeners check the transport peer address against the service address. An optional dci_github_tools: false clears only the DCI container's GitHub token during provisioning, disabling upstream tool registration. Optional agent_guidance is appended to the instance identity at init. An operator can set github_git_only: true to reserve repository changes for inspected HTTPS Git pushes. The proxy checks the HTTP method and route on both GitHub hosts and uses graphql-core to parse GitHub GraphQL operations. Queries and explicitly supported PR, review and comment mutations can pass the content checks. Other repository writes are refused before connecting upstream. The generated policy directory includes the parser and its license. Allowlists, CA private keys and egress audit records live outside the workspace. Each workload joins the namespace of a separate rootless network guard. Only that guard has NET_ADMIN there. Its nftables queues inspect outbound DNS and new connections. Direct packets to unauthorized destinations reach a dummy interface route, are audited, and are rejected in the output hook. If the queue consumer is unavailable the kernel drops queued packets. Internal DNS aliases for allowed hosts point direct HTTPS clients to a second mitmproxy listener. Both listeners enforce the same SNI and HTTP policy. For CNI bridges without DNS, --egress-subnet pins the internal service addresses and installs those aliases in the namespace owners' hosts files. The guard then refuses external DNS. On kernels without a dummy interface driver it routes refused traffic toward a disconnected veth pair. On runc, keep-id workloads join their guard's user namespace to support sysfs and container health checks with the original UID mapping.

The identifier check was replayed against all 63 public dcibot issue comments on redhatci/ansible-collection-redhatci-ocp from 25 November 2026 06:19 UTC through 26 November 18:33 UTC. The 26 even-ID comments included the one reported incident, detected as internal-ticket. The 37 odd-ID holdouts produced zero alerts (zero false positives against the incident report). Four held-back PR descriptions by the same author (#1143–1146) also passed. Run python tests/replay_egress_corpus.py with GitHub CLI access to replay the labels. The fixture stores comment IDs and hashes, so changed or missing published bodies fail the replay. Reversed and base64-transformed secrets are outside the detector's coverage.

Isolated instances via podman-compose with per-service credential isolation: each MCP server runs in its own container and only receives its own secrets. The ai-assist container never sees MCP server credentials.

  • SSE transport: MCP servers connect via SSE (MCPServerConfig.url) instead of stdio; _transport() in agent.py selects it.
  • Instance directory: $AI_ASSIST_INSTANCES_DIR/<name>/ with host-only compose.yaml/.env and a bind-mounted sandbox/ directory.
  • Readiness: _wait_for_mcp_servers() polls TCP ports before launching.
  • CLI: ai-assist /sandbox init|run|stop|list|delete|service.
  • Features: --features=ssh,gpg,git,gh,dci,dbus,litellm,web (default git,dci,vertex; web enables internal__web_search/web_fetch, off otherwise so an autonomous agent cannot send private work to search providers). Vertex AI (gcloud) is always included.
  • litellm feature: a sidecar fronting non-Anthropic models (Gemini, OpenAI) behind the Anthropic Messages dialect; auto-wires ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/AI_ASSIST_API_KEY so the container only sees LITELLM_MASTER_KEY. Aliases live in sandbox/.ai-assist/litellm_config.yaml (copied from sandbox_templates/litellm_config.yaml); see litellm-proxy/README.md.
  • dci feature downloads: both containers mount sandbox/dci-files at /tmp/dci, the server's user (1001) is mapped to the host user (userns_mode: keep-id:uid=1001,gid=1001), /tmp/dci is an allowed path, and DCI_DOWNLOAD_DIR_SHARED=true lets the server pre-download at render time in SSE mode.
  • Timezone: --timezone= sets TZ on every container (default: the host's; --timezone= keeps the image's UTC). It decides when scheduled actions fire (the scheduler compares against a naive datetime.now() and ignores a trigger's own timezone) and keeps one clock across shared files and logs.
  • Image profiles: --image=ai-assist-dev; profile Dockerfiles in sandbox/profiles/ extend the base image and must not set USER (it breaks userns_mode: keep-id).
  • Service mode: ai-assist /sandbox service <name> install|remove|start|stop|status|logs wraps the compose stack as a systemd user service running /monitor; boot startup needs loginctl enable-linger $USER.
  • No pods: --in-pod=false, so each container has its own user namespace. The ai-assist container uses userns_mode: keep-id; MCP server containers run as their default user.
  • Read-only mounts: sandbox_mounts.py implements /sandbox mount add|remove|list, binding existing host directories read-only and updating allowed paths. Sources with writable aliases are refused. Git, credentials, content updates and workflow locks belong to the orchestration layer. Changing mounts requires container recreation.

The DCI MCP server image is built from upstream Containerfile.sse; the ai-assist image from sandbox/ai-assist/Dockerfile. The --timezone default comes from the host's /etc/localtime.

Testing: tests/test_sandbox.py mocks subprocess (default suite). tests/test_sandbox_integration.py starts real containers and is run with make test-integration before merging sandbox changes.

Files: sandbox.py, sandbox_templates/, config.py (MCPServerConfig.url).

docs.title: Event-driven actions
docs.text:
Everything is a trigger + prompt stored in ~/.ai-assist/event-schedules.json and managed via agent tools.

  • ActionDefinition (action_model.py) — unified model replacing TaskDefinition + ScheduledAction.
  • TriggerMatcher (action_model.py) — matches incoming events.
  • ActionEngine (action_engine.py) — executes actions (natural language, MCP prompts, AWL, builtins) with event context.
  • ActionScheduler (action_scheduler.py) — unified scheduler for timer, event and one-shot actions. Edits hot-reload it: FileWatchdog collapses a burst of writes into one callback (debounce state on the loop thread; a running callback is never cancelled), and reload() is serialized by a lock, since overlapping reloads would leave untracked duplicate timers.
  • ActionLoader (action_loader.py) — load/save, auto-migration.
  • ActionTools (action_tools.py) — agent CRUD tools.
  • EventSource ABC (event_sources.py) — MQTT (ai-assist[mqtt]), D-Bus (ai-assist[dbus]), file/glob (watchdog, no extra deps). MQTT pulls in aiomqtt, D-Bus in dbus-next.

Configuration shape and examples are in README § Event-Driven Actions and docs/SCHEDULED_ACTIONS.md. Notes for implementers:

  • One-time actions created with internal__schedule_action (or internal__create_action) run once, then move to event-schedules-archive.jsonl with completed/failed status, matched by name and time. Each (re)load also archives finished ones and those past due beyond the 24 h catch-up window (expired) — see ActionLoader.archive_actions.
  • A "reminder": true action notifies with the prompt text and makes no model call.
  • Event-based actions debounce bursts (3 s); payload_contains / payload_regex filter before execution.
  • Recent notifications from /monitor (last 15 min) are added to the interactive agent's per-query context, so follow-up questions work.

docs.title: Background tasks (interactive mode)
docs.text:
Long-running queries run as background asyncio tasks in the same event loop; the user keeps chatting. A finished task's result is handed back once (BackgroundTaskManager.take_finished_note()): an idle, empty prompt is ended so the agent reports at once (wake_idle_prompt in tui_interactive.py), otherwise the result goes out with the next message. NotificationWatcher still shows completion to the user.

  • background_tasks.py — spawn/track/cancel, in-memory only.
  • background_task_tools.py — internal__run_background, internal__list_background_tasks, internal__get_background_task, internal__cancel_background_task.
  • Isolation: prompts are prefixed @no-kg @no-history plus a note that the answer goes back to the main conversation and nobody can answer questions. Shared MCP sessions are reused. A background task cannot start another.
  • Security: in_background_task() (a ContextVar set in the task's own asyncio task) auto-denies the confirmation prompts of background tasks only; foreground prompts are still asked.
  • Not handed back: cancelled tasks, and tasks spawned with notify_agent=False (MCP channel replies, which answer through their own tool).

docs.title: Configuration, state and cost
docs.text:
Configuration precedence: environment (.env) → ~/.ai-assist/mcp_servers.yaml → identity.yaml → variables.yaml (AWL locals, auto-injected) → event-schedules.json.

Hot-reload (config_watcher.py, file_watchdog.py): config changes reload without restart; monitor mode restarts actions when event-schedules.json changes.

setup_logging() logs the source commit of the ai-assist checkout (with "(uncommitted changes)" when tracked files changed), or nothing when it does not run from its own git checkout (get_source_commit() in config.py).

State in ~/.ai-assist/: knowledge_graph.db, state/, allowed_commands.json, skill_env.json, audit/tool_calls.jsonl, traces/query_traces.jsonl, traces/requests/, events.jsonl, interactive_history.txt. The audit trail is append-only, rotates at 10 MB, and keeps rotated files 7 days; query traces are kept 100 days; captured requests only exist with AI_ASSIST_CAPTURE_MODEL_REQUESTS=true (mode 0600, never pruned).

Cost tracking (pricing.py, eval.py):

  • Prices are not available from the API. MODEL_PRICING is hardcoded and must be updated when rates change (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models).
  • _track_token_usage() records cost per turn; QueryTrace.total_cost_usd aggregates per query. /cost [period] and /eval-stats recompute each query's cost from per-turn counts (QueryTrace.cost_usd()), so old traces are reported correctly; the stored total_cost_usd is used only when per-turn counts are missing or the model has no price.
  • The API's input_tokens excludes cached tokens: compute_turn_cost bills uncached input, cache writes, cache reads and output separately. Anything measuring context fullness (observation masking, the budget warning, get_context_usage) uses prompt_tokens(), the sum of the three input counts.

Prompt caching (AI_ASSIST_ENABLE_CACHE, on by default): the static system block and the last two user messages of each request are marked (_with_message_cache_breakpoints in agent.py); the markers go on a copy, the conversation is never modified. The system prompt must stay byte-identical across queries: the clock, recent notifications and KG learnings/auto-context are appended to the current user turn as a separate block (_build_query_context, _with_query_context), and the breakpoint goes on the user's own text before it, so the next query hits the cache at the same position. Each turn's token entry records prefix_sha (tools + system); workflows/self-improvement/lib/audit-cache.py reports misses.

MLflow (mlflow_tracing.py): optional (pip install ai-assist[mlflow], mlflow-skinny + sqlalchemy), enabled with AI_ASSIST_ENABLE_MLFLOW=true. MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI selects the backend; unset means a local SQLite store at <config dir>/mlflow.db. Emits a query → tool span tree and mirrors QueryTrace metrics. No-op when disabled. The JSONL cost tracking is unaffected.

docs.title: Tools architecture
docs.text:
Built-in tools by domain: report_tools.py, action_tools.py, schedule_action_tools.py, knowledge_tools.py, kg_query_tools.py, filesystem_tools.py (execute_command reports per-stage PIPESTATUS and saves oversized output in the session tmpdir), think_tool.py, json_tools.py, transform_tools.py, introspection_tools.py. MCP tools are prefixed with the server name.

Progressive disclosure (tool_disclosure.py, AI_ASSIST_DEFER_TOOLS, on by default): only CORE_TOOLS are sent in full; every other tool, MCP or internal, is listed in the description of introspection__call_tool, read with introspection__get_tool_help and called through that proxy. The tool list never changes, so the prompt cache and thinking signatures stay valid. Choose CORE_TOOLS from audit trails, not by guess. Skills work the same way: only their front matter is in the system prompt. A proxied call is validated against the tool's schema (check_arguments, strict) before it runs; an invalid call is not executed and the error carries the tool's documentation. last_tool_calls records what ran this query.

Agent collaborators: tool_result_router.py (ToolResultRouter, result redirection and pagination), synthesis_engine.py (SynthesisEngine, synthesis, _save_insights, KG connection discovery), system_prompt_builder.py (SystemPromptBuilder, system prompt and per-query context). Each holds an agent back-reference and reads collaborators live; AiAssistAgent keeps thin delegating wrappers for the names tests and other modules use.

Result redirection: every tool accepts __save_to_file, __write_to_report, __append_to_report, __collect_to_report (auto-paginate and collect, needs server pagination config) and __jq_filter (runs first).

Dedup and loop detection (_execute_tools_concurrently in agent.py): identical calls (name + args) within a query are served from a result cache; a signature repeated ≥3× in the last 5 triggers loop detection (first offense nudges, a second aborts). Poll-safe tools — async status checks expected to be called repeatedly — are exempt: list fnmatch patterns in AI_ASSIST_REPEATABLE_TOOLS (whitespace/comma separated, config.repeatable_tools), matched by AiAssistAgent._is_repeatable_tool. A repeatable tool bypasses the cache and is never loop-flagged.

Audit: each _execute_tool call runs inside audited_call() (audit.py, a ContextVar, so concurrent calls stay separate), which assigns the correlation_id and collects authorization events (record_authorization_event — approval prompts via FilesystemTools._record_confirmation, policy refusals of paths, commands and protected configs, plan mode) and lets one record through per call. See SECURITY.md §6 for the record format, rotation and AI_ASSIST_AUDIT_SINK.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Agent Workflow Language (AWL) is a lightweight scripting language used to orchestrate AI agent workflows.

AWL focuses on intent-driven orchestration rather than explicit tool invocation.

Instead of specifying which tools to call, AWL scripts define:

  • goals
  • workflow structure
  • conditions
  • loops
  • variable propagation

The agent remains responsible for selecting tools and strategies to accomplish each task.

This design keeps AWL:

  • human readable
  • LLM-friendly
  • flexible
  • safe

docs.title: Intent-driven workflows
docs.text: Scripts describe what must be achieved, not how to implement it.

docs.title: Agent autonomy
docs.text:
The agent determines:

  • which tools to use
  • how to search or analyze
  • when a task is complete

docs.title: Minimal syntax
docs.text: The language remains simple so that both humans and LLMs can easily produce and edit scripts.

docs.title: Deterministic structure
docs.text: Although the agent reasons dynamically, the workflow structure is deterministic and validated by the runtime.

docs.title: Script Structure
docs.text:
An AWL script begins with @start and ends with @end.

Example:

@start

@task find_server Goal: Find where the HTTP server is initialized. Success: Identify the file and function responsible for startup. Expose: server_file, server_function @end

@end

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
AWL defines the following directives.

Directive Description @start start workflow @end end block @task define agent task @set assign variable @if conditional execution @else alternate branch @loop iterate collection @continue skip current loop iteration @break exit loop early @return return workflow result @goal autonomous goal pursuit

docs.title: Task Hints
docs.text:
Tasks may include execution hints placed after the task name.

Hints influence the context available to the agent, but do not prescribe specific tools.

Example:

@task fresh_search @no-history @no-kg Goal: Re-evaluate where the HTTP server is initialized. Success: Identify the startup path using only repository evidence. Expose: server_file, server_function @end

docs.title: @no-history
docs.text:
The agent must ignore prior conversation history and previous reasoning context.

This ensures that the task is evaluated with a fresh reasoning context.

Example:

@task fresh_analysis @no-history Goal: Analyze the repository structure without using previous conclusions. @end

docs.title: @no-kg
docs.text:
The agent must not consult the external knowledge graph or knowledge base.

Only live data sources such as repository inspection or runtime tools may be used.

Example:

@task repository_only @no-kg Goal: Determine how the system initializes using only source code evidence. @end

docs.title: max_tool_calls=N and max_time=N
docs.text:
max_tool_calls overrides the default tool call budget (100) for a single task. The budget is soft: when it is reached, the agent is told to wrap up and gets up to 50% more tool calls.

max_time sets a wall-clock budget, in seconds, for a single task. Without it, a task has no time limit (only a stalled model connection is cut off).

When either budget runs out, the agent is not cut off mid-work: it gets one final turn in which it can only call internal__finish_task, to report success with what it has or failure with what is missing.

Use this when a task may need many tool calls, such as running a detailed analysis before creating a ticket.

Example:

@task analyze_and_report max_tool_calls=200 max_time=1800 Goal: Run a root cause analysis on the job and create a Jira ticket. Expose: jira_ticket @end

docs.title: model=\<level>
docs.text:
model selects an abstract capability level for a single task, so scripts stay provider-neutral. The valid values are low, medium, high, and default. Use a lower level for cheap/mechanical work and a higher level for deep analysis. A task with no model= uses default (the session model).

Each level maps to a concrete model via env vars:

level env var fallback when unset low AI_ASSIST_MODEL_LOW default medium AI_ASSIST_MODEL_MEDIUM default high AI_ASSIST_MODEL_HIGH default default AI_ASSIST_MODEL high, then claude-sonnet-4-6

default is the session model — the same one used for interactive sessions and set by --model. default and high fall back to each other: set only AI_ASSIST_MODEL and high tracks it; set only AI_ASSIST_MODEL_HIGH and the session model tracks that (so a config that defines only the AWL levels still runs on a sensible model). Set both explicitly to make them differ.

Model environment values may include an effort suffix, for example AI_ASSIST_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6:medium or AI_ASSIST_MODEL_HIGH=claude-opus-4-6:max. A recognized suffix (low, medium, high, xhigh, max, or no) is removed from the model ID and becomes that model's effort; no means send no effort, for a model that rejects the parameter. A tier (AI_ASSIST_MODEL_LOW/_MEDIUM/_HIGH) without its own suffix inherits the session effort; :no opts it out. Explicit AI_ASSIST_EFFORT and --effort values take precedence. Unrecognized suffixes are preserved as part of the model ID for custom providers.

The value is validated at workflow load time. Any value other than low, medium, high, or default (including a concrete model id) fails the workflow before any task executes.

Example:

@task search_jobs model=low @no-kg Goal: Search DCI for failed jobs in the last 24 hours. Expose: failed_jobs @end

@task root_cause model=high Goal: Perform root cause analysis on ${failed_jobs}. Expose: rca_result @end

docs.title:
@continue-on-failure

By default, if a top-level task (outside a loop) fails, the workflow stops immediately and returns success: false. This prevents cascading errors from missing variables.

Tasks inside loops are not affected — loop iterations that fail are skipped, and the loop continues to the next item.

The @continue-on-failure hint overrides the default fail-fast behavior, allowing the workflow to continue even if the task fails.

Example:

@task optional_cleanup @continue-on-failure Goal: Clean up temporary files. Not critical if this fails. @end
Tasks
docs.text:
Tasks represent objectives for the agent.

Syntax:

@task [hints...] [max_tool_calls=N] [max_time=N] [model=] [effort=] ... @end

Example:

@task locate_config Goal: Find where the server configuration is loaded. Context: Focus on startup code and configuration parsing. Success: Identify the entrypoint and parser. Expose: config_entrypoint, config_parser @end

docs.title: Task Fields
docs.text:
Inside a task block the following fields may appear.

Field Purpose Goal task objective Context additional context Constraints optional limitations Success completion criteria Expose variables produced

docs.title:
Shell Commands in Tasks

When a task requires the agent to run a specific shell command, enclose it in backticks:

@task update_repo Goal: Fetch the latest changes using git -C /path/to/repo fetch origin master. @end

Commands in backticks are auto-authorized by the runtime: they are temporarily added to the allowed commands list for the duration of the workflow, so the user is not prompted for confirmation each time.

This only applies to scripts the user started: ai-assist /run, and actions (internal__create_action) whose AWL prompt the user confirmed. When the agent runs a script itself (introspection__execute_awl_script), its commands go through the normal allowlist and confirmation — unless an action is running whose own prompt names that script (e.g. "1. Run ~/flows/weekly.awl with days=7. 2. Email the report."): creating such an action asks for the same confirmation, and the script then runs as if it were the action's prompt. Only the action's prompt counts, not the event data added to it, and the paths must match once resolved. If the last run of such a script failed, the action is reported as failed even when the agent carries on and ends normally.

Commands are taken from the script text, never from interpolated values. A ${var} may only choose a directory, with the script name written literally (${tools_dir}/build.sh), and its value must be a plain path (no spaces or shell syntax).

Commands written without backticks will require manual authorization in interactive mode.
Variables
docs.text:
Variables can be defined using @set.

Example:

@set target = "HTTP server"

Variables can be referenced using interpolation:

${target}

Example:

Goal: Find where ${target} is initialized.

docs.title:
Initial Variables

Variables can be injected before the script runs, without needing @set.

From the CLI:

ai-assist /run workflow.awl target="HTTP server" days=7

From an agent prompt: ask the agent to run a .awl file and it will call the introspection__execute_awl_script tool with the variables you specify.

Injected variables are available from the first node, just like @set variables.

Built-in Variables

AWL automatically injects built-in variables into every execution. These are available without any CLI arguments or @set directives.

Date/time (generated fresh per execution):

Variable Example Description date 2026-07-17 Local date time 14:30:05 Local time datetime 2026-07-17 14:30:05 Local date+time utc_date 2026-07-17 UTC date utc_time 12:30:05 UTC time utc_datetime 2026-07-17 12:30:05 UTC date+time timezone CEST Local timezone abbreviation

Paths:

Variable Description config_dir Config directory (~/.ai-assist) reports_dir Reports directory (~/ai-assist/reports) logs_dir Logs directory (~/.ai-assist/logs) tmpdir Session-scoped temporary directory (created at startup, cleaned up on exit) source_dir Top directory of the ai-assist source tree (parent of the ai_assist package) script_path Absolute path of the running .awl script script_dir Absolute directory containing the running .awl script

User-Defined Variables (variables.yaml)

Define custom variables in ~/.ai-assist/variables.yaml to make them available in all AWL scripts. This makes scripts location-independent — different users can run the same script with their own settings.

workspace: ~/ai-assist/workspace
team: dci
jira_project: CILAB

Values support ~ expansion and $ENV_VAR substitution. The file is optional.

Precedence (highest wins):

  1. CLI / caller-provided variables (ai-assist /run script.awl key=value)
  2. User-defined variables from variables.yaml
  3. Built-in variables (date/time, paths)

Variable Validation

AWL performs static analysis before execution to detect variables that are used before they are defined. This catches common mistakes such as:

  • Typos in variable names (e.g., @if failure_count > 0 when only failed_jobs was exposed)
  • Referencing a collect variable inside the loop that produces it (the collect variable is only available after the loop)
  • Using ${var} in a task goal when no prior task exposed that variable

Validation warnings are reported in three places:

  1. inspect_awl_script — included as variable_warnings in the result
  2. execute_awl_script — blocks execution and returns an error
  3. Runtime — printed to the console before execution starts
Scoping rules
docs.text: Source Available where @set All subsequent nodes Expose: All subsequent nodes @loop ... as item Inside the loop body collect=var After the loop (not inside the body) Initial variables Everywhere

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text: A task fails when its model call fails (API error such as a rate limit, or a stalled model stream): the error is never taken as the task's answer. Like any task failure, this stops the workflow unless the task has @continue-on-failure.

docs.title:
Reporting the task outcome

During a task, and only then, the agent has an internal__finish_task tool. The task prompt asks it to call the tool once when done:

  • status="success" with values holding the task's Expose: variables. These are taken as is (method finish_tool); only keys missing from values go through the usual extraction (JSON block in the reply, nudge, report sections).
  • status="failed" with a reason when the goal could not be achieved (a required step failed, a tool returned an error, needed data is missing). The task then fails with that reason, exactly like any other task failure, instead of exposing empty values that later steps would take as real results.

When a task runs out of its turn budget (max_tool_calls, after the extra wrap-up turns) or its max_time, it gets a final turn in which only internal__finish_task is offered. It fails as unfinished ("stopped before finishing") only if it still doesn't report.

If the agent ends its turn without calling the tool (typically narrating a next step, like "Now writing the report.", and stopping), it is nudged once to continue or report. If it still doesn't call it, the task behaves as before: success, with values extracted from its reply. A value that isn't in the reply stays unset (None) rather than being guessed.

@fail

Aborts the workflow immediately with an error message.

Syntax:

@fail

Example — abort unconditionally:

@fail Jira server is in maintenance

Example — abort when a task did not produce the expected result:

@if not jira_report @fail Jira collection failed - aborting quarterly review @end

The error is reported to the caller, with ${var} references in the message interpolated. Combine with @if/@else for conditional abort vs. alternative path.

Agent guidance: When a task's upstream service is unavailable or returns an error, do NOT expose the expected variables — leave them unset. The script can then detect the failure with @if not <variable> and abort with @fail.

@continue

Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next item (like Python's continue). Only valid inside @loop or @while blocks. Outside a loop, behaves like @fail.

Syntax:

@continue

The message is required and supports ${variable} interpolation. It is logged for debugging. When used inside a @loop with collect=, skipped iterations contribute nothing to the collected results.

Example — skip a loop iteration when a task returns unexpected state:

@loop pull_requests as pr @task checkout_branch goal: Check out the branch for PR ${pr.number}. Expose: branch_ready @end @if branch_ready == 'unknown' @continue checkout nudged -- branch state unknown, skipping PR ${pr.number} @end @task analyze_pr goal: Analyze the PR. @end @end

@break

Exits the enclosing loop immediately (like Python's break). Only valid inside @loop or @while blocks. Outside a loop, behaves like @fail.

Syntax:

@break

The message is required and supports ${variable} interpolation. When used inside a @loop with collect=, items collected before @break are preserved.

Example — stop processing after finding the first match:

@loop candidates as candidate @task evaluate goal: Evaluate ${candidate}. Expose: score @end @if score > 90 @set winner ${candidate} @break found a winner with score ${score} @end @end
Nested loops
docs.text:
@continue and @break only affect the innermost enclosing loop (same semantics as Python). To exit an outer loop from inside a nested loop, use a variable:

@set done = false @loop repos as repo @if not done @loop branches as branch @task check Goal: Check ${repo} ${branch}. Expose: found @end @if found @set done = true @break found target in ${repo}/${branch} @end @end @end @end

docs.title: Conditional Execution
docs.text:
Syntax:

@if ... @else ... @end

Example:

@if handlers

@task analyze_handlers Goal: Understand the detected handlers. Expose: handler_summaries @end

@else

@task search_handlers Goal: Search more broadly for request entry points. Expose: handlers @end

@end

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Expressions are intentionally simple.

Supported operations:

Expression Example variable handlers negation not report_exists property config.entrypoint index handlers[0] length len(handlers) comparison len(handlers) > 0 string literal status == 'unknown'

String literals use single or double quotes ('value' or "value"). Smart/curly quotes are automatically normalized to straight quotes. Comparison operators: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Loops iterate over collections.

Syntax:

@loop as [limit=N] [collect=[()]] ... @end

The optional limit=N parameter caps the number of iterations.

docs.title:
Collecting Results

The optional collect=<var> parameter accumulates exposed variables from each successful iteration into a list.

Example:

@loop handlers as handler limit=5 collect=summaries

@task inspect_handler Goal: Understand what ${handler} does. Expose: handler_summary, handler_priority @end

@end

After the loop, summaries contains:

[ {"handler_summary": "...", "handler_priority": "high"}, {"handler_summary": "...", "handler_priority": "low"} ]

To collect only specific fields, use parentheses:

@loop handlers as handler collect=summaries(handler_summary)

This produces:

[ {"handler_summary": "..."}, {"handler_summary": "..."} ]

Failed iterations are skipped and do not appear in the collected list.

Important: The collect variable is only available after the loop completes. Referencing it inside the loop body (e.g., ${summaries} in a task goal) will trigger a validation error, because the variable has not been populated yet.

Basic Loop

Example without collect:

@loop handlers as handler limit=5

@task inspect_handler Goal: Understand what ${handler} does. Expose: handler_summary @end

@end
Conditional Loop
docs.text:
@while repeats its body while an expression is truthy.

Syntax:

@while [max_iterations=N] ... @end

The optional max_iterations=N parameter limits the number of iterations (default: 100) as a safety guard against infinite loops.

Example:

@while running_count > 0 max_iterations=24

@task check_status @no-history @no-kg Goal: Count running DCI jobs. Do NOT fetch details. Expose: running_count @end

@end

Tasks inside @while do not count against the workflow's max_steps limit, since iteration count is already bounded by max_iterations.

docs.title: Wait
docs.text:
@wait pauses execution for a specified duration.

Syntax:

@wait s|m|h

Examples:

@wait 30s @wait 5m @wait 1h

Useful for rate-limiting API calls or spacing out polling iterations.

docs.title: Notify
docs.text:
@notify emits a user-facing message with variable interpolation. No agent call is made — this is a pure runtime operation.

Syntax:

@notify

Example:

@notify ${running_count} jobs still running @notify All daily DCI jobs have completed

docs.title: Return
docs.text:
Workflows can return a result.

@return handlers

docs.title: Polling Example
docs.text:
This workflow polls for running DCI jobs, notifies progress, and exits when done:

@start

@task check_jobs @no-history @no-kg Goal: Search for daily DCI jobs still running. Count them. Expose: running_count @end

@while running_count > 0 max_iterations=24

@notify ${running_count} DCI jobs still running

@wait 1h

@task recheck_jobs @no-history @no-kg @continue-on-failure Goal: Search for daily DCI jobs still running. Count them. Expose: running_count @end

@end

@notify All daily DCI jobs have completed

@end

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
@start

@task find_handlers @no-kg Goal: Find HTTP handlers defined in the repository. Expose: handlers @end

@if len(handlers) > 0

@loop handlers as handler limit=5

@task inspect_handler @no-history Goal: Understand what ${handler} does. Expose: handler_summary @end

@end

@else

@task fallback_search Goal: Search more broadly for request entry points. Expose: handlers @end

@end

@return handlers

@end

docs.title: Runtime Architecture
docs.text:
The runtime contains four main components.

Component Responsibility Workflow Engine executes AWL scripts Agent performs reasoning Tool Runtime executes tools safely Memory System stores workflow state

Execution pipeline:

AWL Script ↓ Parser ↓ Workflow AST ↓ Runtime Engine ↓ Agent reasoning loop ↓ Tool execution ↓ Memory updates

docs.title: Task Execution Model
docs.text:
Each task runs an agent reasoning loop.

Lifecycle:

task start ↓ build task context ↓ agent reasoning loop ↓ success detection ↓ store exposed variables ↓ task end

docs.title: Task Context
docs.text:
Before executing a task, the runtime builds a context object.

Example:

{ "task_id": "find_server", "goal": "Find where the HTTP server is initialized.", "success": "Identify the file and function responsible for startup.", "expose": ["server_file","server_function"], "variables": {} }

Hints such as @no-history and @no-kg are included in this context.

docs.title: Task Outcomes
docs.text:
A task may terminate with one of several outcomes.

Status Meaning success goal achieved failed task attempted but not successful blocked task cannot proceed due to missing dependency aborted execution intentionally stopped

Example success result:

{ "status": "success", "summary": "Server initialized in cmd/server/main.go", "exposed": { "server_file": "cmd/server/main.go" } }

Example blocked result:

{ "status": "blocked", "reason": "repository_not_loaded", "message": "Cannot analyze repository because none is loaded." }

docs.title: Runtime Limits
docs.text:
Safety limits enforced by the runtime.

Limit Purpose max_steps maximum reasoning steps max_tool_calls maximum tool executions timeout maximum task duration

Example configuration:

max_steps = 12 max_tool_calls = 20 timeout = 30s

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
Goals enable autonomous agent behavior by scheduling periodic execution of an AWL body.

Syntax:

@goal [max_actions=] Success: @end Parameters: | Parameter | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | max_actions | no | Max tool calls per cycle (default: 5) | Scheduling is independent from the goal definition. Goals can be run: - From the CLI: `ai-assist /run goal.awl` - Via `event-schedules.json`: `{"prompt": "goals/track_failures.awl", "trigger": {"type": "interval", "every": "30m"}}` - As a one-shot scheduled action The `Success:` field is mandatory. After each cycle, Claude evaluates whether the criterion is met. When met, the goal status is set to "completed" and scheduling stops. ## Variable Persistence Variables exposed by tasks inside the goal body persist between cycles via a JSON sidecar file. This allows the goal to track state across executions. ## Example @start @goal track_failures max_actions=5 Success: Failure rate stays below 10% @task check_status @no-history Goal: Check DCI failure rate for OCP 4.19. Expose: failure_rate, failures @end @if failure_rate > 10 @task create_alert Goal: Write a failure report about ${failures}. @end @end @end @end ## Goal Files Goal AWL scripts live in `~/.ai-assist/goals/`. The monitor mode scans this directory and schedules active goals. State is persisted in `~/.ai-assist/state/goal_.json`. ## Goal Management The agent can create, list, and update goals via built-in tools: - `goal__create` -- generates a `.awl` file - `goal__list` -- scans the goals directory - `goal__update` -- changes goal status (pause, resume, cancel) --- # Summary The Agent Workflow Language enables structured orchestration of AI agents. Key properties: - intent-driven workflows - agent autonomy - task hints controlling context - deterministic execution - extensible architecture ## Implementation notes Task completion (`internal__finish_task`), model-tier and effort resolution, the auto-authorization rules for backticked commands, and audit attribution are described in [ARCHITECTURE § AWL](ARCHITECTURE.md#awl).

docs.title: Identity Configuration
docs.text: The identity.yaml file allows you to personalize how ai-assist interacts with you by customizing the assistant's behavior, your information, and communication preferences.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
The identity file is located at: 

~/.ai-assist/identity.yaml

Or if using a custom config directory: 

$AI_ASSIST_CONFIG_DIR/identity.yaml

docs.title: Auto-Reload
docs.text: Changes to identity.yaml are automatically detected and applied without restarting ai-assist in both monitor and interactive modes.

docs.title: Configuration Structure
docs.text: The identity file has three main sections: user, assistant, and preferences.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
version: '1.0'

user:
  name: 'Alex'
  role: 'DevOps Engineer'
  organization: 'Acme Corp'
  timezone: 'America/New_York'
  context: |
    I work on the Cloud Platform team, focusing on CI/CD pipelines
    and infrastructure automation. My priorities are reliability,
    security, and developer experience.

assistant:
  nickname: 'Nexus'
  personality: |
    You are Nexus, a helpful AI assistant specialized in DevOps
    and cloud infrastructure. You provide clear, actionable advice
    and focus on best practices for reliability and security.

preferences:
  formality: 'professional'
  verbosity: 'concise'
  emoji_usage: 'moderate'

docs.title: User Section
docs.text: Configure information about yourself that the assistant will use for personalization.

docs.title: user.name (string, default: "there")
docs.text:
Your name. Used in greetings and personalized responses.

Examples: 

name: 'Alex'
name: 'Sarah Chen'

docs.title: user.role (string, optional)
docs.text:
Your job title or role.

Examples: 

role: 'DevOps Engineer'
role: 'Site Reliability Engineer'
role: 'Platform Architect'

docs.title: user.organization (string, optional)
docs.text:
Your company or organization name.

Examples: 

organization: 'Acme Corp'
organization: 'Red Hat'

docs.title: user.timezone (string, optional)
docs.text:
Your timezone (not currently used in logic, but stored for context).

Examples: 

timezone: 'America/New_York'
timezone: 'Europe/Paris'
timezone: 'UTC'

docs.title: user.context (string, optional)
docs.text:
Detailed information about your work context, team structure, priorities, or anything else you want the assistant to know about your environment. This is added to the system prompt.

Examples: 

context: |
  I work on the OpenShift CI/CD team, focusing on pipeline
  reliability and test infrastructure. My main priorities are
  reducing flaky tests and improving developer feedback loops.


context: |
  Engineering Manager for the Storage team at Red Hat.
  Responsible for Ceph and OpenShift Data Foundation.
  Team of 8 engineers across 3 time zones.

docs.title: Assistant Section
docs.text: Customize the assistant's identity and behavior.

docs.title: assistant.nickname (string, default: "Nexus")
docs.text:
The name the assistant uses to identify itself.

Examples: 

nickname: 'Nexus'
nickname: 'Atlas'
nickname: 'Helios'

docs.title: assistant.personality (string, optional)
docs.text:
A custom system prompt that completely overrides the default personality. Use this for specialized behavior or domain expertise.

Warning: When set, this replaces the entire default personality. If not set, a personality is automatically generated from other fields.

Examples: 

personality: |
  You are Atlas, an AI assistant specialized in Kubernetes and
  cloud-native technologies. You provide expert guidance on
  container orchestration, service mesh, and GitOps practices.
  You always consider security and scalability in your advice.


personality: |
  You are Helios, a friendly AI assistant focused on helping
  with DCI (Distributed CI) workflows. You're familiar with
  OpenShift testing, CI/CD pipelines, and test result analysis.
  You communicate clearly and help troubleshoot test failures.

docs.title: Preferences Section
docs.text: Control the assistant's communication style.

docs.title: preferences.formality (string, default: "professional")
docs.text:
How formal the assistant should be in responses.

Options: - professional - Maintains a professional, business-appropriate tone - casual - Communicates in a casual, friendly manner - friendly - Warm and approachable, but still helpful

Examples: 

formality: 'professional'  # "I recommend reviewing the logs for errors."
formality: 'casual'        # "Let's check the logs for any errors."
formality: 'friendly'      # "I'd be happy to help you check the logs!"

docs.title: preferences.verbosity (string, default: "concise")
docs.text:
How detailed responses should be.

Options: - concise - Brief, to-the-point responses - detailed - Provides detailed explanations when appropriate - verbose - Comprehensive, thorough explanations

Examples: 

verbosity: 'concise'   # "The test failed due to timeout."
verbosity: 'detailed'  # "The test failed because it exceeded the 5-minute timeout. This suggests the service is slow to respond."
verbosity: 'verbose'   # "The test failed due to a timeout after 5 minutes. This typically indicates... [continues with detailed explanation]"

docs.title: preferences.emoji_usage (string, default: "moderate")
docs.text:
How frequently emojis are used in responses.

Options: - none - No emojis - minimal - Only when they add clarity - moderate - Occasionally to enhance communication - liberal - Frequent emoji usage for engagement

Examples: 

emoji_usage: 'none'     # "Test passed."
emoji_usage: 'minimal'  # "Test passed ✓"
emoji_usage: 'moderate' # "✅ Test passed"
emoji_usage: 'liberal'  # "🎉 Test passed! ✅"

docs.title: Minimal Configuration
docs.text:
Just the basics:

version: '1.0'
user:
  name: 'Your Name'

docs.title: Professional Setup
docs.text:
For enterprise/work environments:

version: '1.0'

user:
  name: 'Your Name'
  role: 'Your Role'
  organization: 'Your Company'

preferences:
  formality: 'professional'
  verbosity: 'concise'
  emoji_usage: 'minimal'

docs.title: Specialized Assistant
docs.text:
For domain-specific expertise:

version: '1.0'

user:
  name: 'Your Name'
  context: |
    Describe your work context, team structure,
    and main responsibilities here.

assistant:
  nickname: 'Atlas'
  personality: |
    You are Atlas, an expert in [your domain]. You provide
    clear, actionable guidance on [specific topics].
    You prioritize [your key values: security, reliability, etc.].

preferences:
  formality: 'professional'
  verbosity: 'detailed'
  emoji_usage: 'moderate'

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
Use the built-in command to create a template:

ai-assist /identity-init

This creates a basic identity.yaml with default values that you can customize.

docs.title: Manual Creation
docs.text:
Create the file at ~/.ai-assist/identity.yaml with your preferred editor:

mkdir -p ~/.ai-assist
cat > ~/.ai-assist/identity.yaml << 'EOF'
version: '1.0'
user:
  name: 'Your Name'
assistant:
  nickname: 'Nexus'
preferences:
  formality: 'professional'
  verbosity: 'concise'
  emoji_usage: 'moderate'
EOF

docs.title: Viewing Your Identity
docs.text:

docs.title: How Identity Affects the Assistant
docs.text:
The identity configuration influences:

  1. System Prompt - The assistant's personality and behavior are set via the system prompt
  2. Greetings - Personalized welcome messages in interactive mode
  3. Context - The assistant is aware of your role, organization, and priorities
  4. Communication - Response style matches your preferences

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start Simple - Begin with just your name and preferences, add more later
  2. Use Context Wisely - Include information that helps the assistant understand your priorities
  3. Match Your Style - Choose preferences that feel natural to you
  4. Iterate - Adjust preferences based on how responses feel
  5. Specialized Assistants - Use custom personality for domain-specific expertise

docs.title: Changes Not Applied
docs.text:
If changes to identity.yaml don't take effect:

  1. Check Syntax - Ensure valid YAML format (use a YAML validator)
  2. Check Location - Verify file is in correct config directory
  3. Restart - In rare cases, restart ai-assist (though auto-reload should work)

docs.title: How to Inspect the Knowledge Base
docs.text: There are three main ways to see what the agent has learned:

docs.title: 1. Ask the Agent (Easiest)
docs.text:
Just talk to the agent in interactive mode:

ai-assist /interactive

docs.title: Check Preferences
docs.text:
You: What preferences do you know about me?

Agent: Let me check... [calls internal__search_knowledge(entity_type="user_preference")]

Agent: I know the following preferences:
  • python_test_framework: You prefer pytest over unittest
  • code_formatter: You use black for Python formatting
  • git_branch_style: You name bug fix branches as bug/TICKET-ID

docs.title: Check Lessons Learned
docs.text:
You: What have you learned about DCI?

Agent: [calls internal__search_knowledge(entity_type="lesson_learned", query="%dci%")]

Agent: I've learned:
  • dci_friday_pattern: DCI jobs fail more on Fridays due to upstream CI runs
  • dci_error_handling: Always check rate limits before bulk operations

docs.title: Useful Queries
docs.text:
List all entity types: 

SELECT entity_type, COUNT(*)
FROM entities
WHERE tx_to IS NULL  -- Only current (not superseded)
GROUP BY entity_type;

View all user preferences: 

SELECT
    id,
    json_extract(data, '$.key') as key,
    json_extract(data, '$.content') as content,
    json_extract(data, '$.metadata.tags') as tags,
    json_extract(data, '$.metadata.confidence') as confidence,
    tx_from as learned_at
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type = 'user_preference'
AND tx_to IS NULL
ORDER BY tx_from DESC;

Search knowledge by content: 

SELECT
    entity_type,
    json_extract(data, '$.key') as key,
    json_extract(data, '$.content') as content
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type IN ('user_preference', 'lesson_learned', 'project_context', 'decision_rationale')
AND json_extract(data, '$.content') LIKE '%python%'
AND tx_to IS NULL;

View knowledge with high confidence: 

SELECT
    entity_type,
    json_extract(data, '$.key') as key,
    json_extract(data, '$.content') as content,
    CAST(json_extract(data, '$.metadata.confidence') AS REAL) as confidence
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type IN ('user_preference', 'lesson_learned', 'project_context', 'decision_rationale')
AND CAST(json_extract(data, '$.metadata.confidence') AS REAL) >= 0.9
AND tx_to IS NULL;

View when knowledge was learned: 

SELECT
    entity_type,
    json_extract(data, '$.key') as key,
    tx_from as learned_at,
    valid_from as became_true_at,
    date(tx_from) as date
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type IN ('user_preference', 'lesson_learned', 'project_context', 'decision_rationale')
AND tx_to IS NULL
ORDER BY tx_from DESC;

docs.title: Understanding the Knowledge Graph Structure
docs.text:
The knowledge graph uses bi-temporal tracking:

  • valid_from / valid_to: When the fact was true in reality
  • tx_from / tx_to: When the agent learned/stopped believing it

This allows you to answer questions like: - "What did I know on January 1st?" (transaction time) - "What was true on January 1st?" (valid time)

docs.title: Entity Types
docs.text:
Knowledge Management: - user_preference: Your stated preferences - lesson_learned: Patterns and insights - project_context: Background information - decision_rationale: Why choices were made

Conversations: - conversation: User/assistant exchanges (saved on-the-fly during interactive sessions) - synthesis_marker: Tracks when KG synthesis last ran

Automatically Captured: - dci_job: DCI jobs from searches - jira_ticket: Jira tickets from searches - dci_component: Components used in DCI jobs

docs.title: Agent Knowledge Management
docs.text:
The ai-assist agent can learn and remember information from conversations.

📖 See also: INSPECTING_KNOWLEDGE.md for detailed instructions on viewing stored knowledge.

docs.title: What Gets Saved
docs.text: The agent automatically saves: - Conversations: Every user/assistant exchange is stored in the Knowledge Graph on-the-fly - User Preferences: Code style, tools, workflows - Lessons Learned: Bug patterns, best practices - Project Context: Goals, constraints, background - Decision Rationale: Why choices were made

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Every conversation exchange is saved to the Knowledge Graph as it happens
  2. Structured knowledge (preferences, lessons, context, rationale) is extracted from the conversation when it is compacted, cleared (/clear), or when you exit an interactive session — each runs as a background task (synchronously on exit) so facts you stated (for example, where a piece of code lives) survive a growing context window and short sessions still contribute
  3. Re-stating a fact updates the existing entry rather than creating a duplicate (semantic key-reuse)
  4. A nightly KG synthesis task (configurable in event-schedules.json) snapshots new/changed reports and discovers connections between entities — it no longer mines conversations
  5. Agent can recall saved knowledge in future conversations

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
You: I prefer pytest over unittest for Python testing
Agent: Got it! I'll remember to use pytest for Python tests.
[Agent saves: user_preference:python_test_framework]

# Next conversation:
You: Write tests for the login function
Agent: I'll write pytest tests for login...
[Agent recalled preference from knowledge base]

docs.title: Access Tracking
docs.text:
Every time the agent recalls knowledge — whether via system prompt injection or explicit search — an access event is recorded. This lets you measure which knowledge is actually useful:

You: How healthy is your knowledge graph?
Agent: [Calls internal__kg_knowledge_health]
Agent:
  Total accesses: 142
  Most accessed: user_preference:python_test_framework (28 times)
  Never accessed: 3 entries
  Stale (>7 days): 2 entries

docs.title: Method 3: Direct Database Query (Advanced)
docs.text:
For advanced users, inspect the SQLite database directly:

# View the database
sqlite3 ~/.ai-assist/knowledge_graph.db

# List all entity types
SELECT entity_type, COUNT(*) FROM entities WHERE tx_to IS NULL GROUP BY entity_type;

# View knowledge entities
SELECT id, entity_type, json_extract(data, '$.content')
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type IN ('user_preference', 'lesson_learned', 'project_context', 'decision_rationale')
AND tx_to IS NULL;

# View a specific preference
SELECT * FROM entities WHERE id LIKE 'user_preference:%';

docs.title: Temporal Queries
docs.text: The Knowledge Graph uses a bi-temporal model — every entry tracks both when it happened in reality (valid_from/valid_to) and when the agent learned about it (tx_from/tx_to). The agent can query knowledge across time:

docs.title: Point-in-Time Snapshots
docs.text:
You: What did you know yesterday at 3pm?
Agent: [Calls internal__kg_snapshot(time="2026-06-28T15:00:00", mode="known_at")]

You: What was happening on June 15?
Agent: [Calls internal__kg_snapshot(time="2026-06-15T00:00:00", mode="valid_at")]

Two modes: - known_at: What the agent believed at that moment (transaction time) - valid_at: What was true in reality at that moment (valid time)

docs.title: Time-Filtered Search
docs.text:
You: What have you learned in the past 2 days?
Agent: [Calls internal__search_knowledge(since="2026-06-27T00:00:00")]

You: Any new lessons since Monday?
Agent: [Calls internal__search_knowledge(entity_type="lesson_learned", since="2026-06-23T00:00:00")]

docs.title: Expiring Knowledge
docs.text:
The agent can mark entries as outdated or incorrect:

You: I switched from vim to neovim
Agent: [Calls internal__expire_knowledge(entity_id="user_preference:editor", reason="no_longer_valid")]
       [Calls internal__save_knowledge(..., content="User uses neovim")]

You: Actually, that lesson about Friday failures was wrong
Agent: [Calls internal__expire_knowledge(entity_id="lesson_learned:dci_friday_failures", reason="retract")]

Two reasons: - no_longer_valid: The fact stopped being true (e.g., user changed preference) - retract: The belief was incorrect (e.g., wrong assumption)

docs.title: Future Knowledge
docs.text:
The agent can store facts that will become true in the future:

You: I'll be at a conference in Berlin on July 10
Agent: [Calls internal__save_knowledge(..., valid_from="2026-07-10")]

Future-dated knowledge is excluded from normal searches and system prompt injection by default — it only surfaces when its valid_from date arrives. The agent can explicitly query future entries:

You: What do you know about my upcoming plans?
Agent: [Calls internal__search_knowledge(include_future=true)]

docs.title: Agent Tools (Internal)
docs.text:
The agent has these internal tools (automatically used, not directly callable):

Knowledge Management: - internal__save_knowledge: Explicitly save facts - internal__search_knowledge: Search for saved learnings (supports since filter) - internal__expire_knowledge: Mark entries as no longer valid or retract incorrect beliefs

Temporal Queries: - internal__kg_snapshot: Query the knowledge graph at a point in time - internal__kg_recent_changes: Get changes in the last N hours - internal__kg_late_discoveries: Find entities discovered late - internal__kg_discovery_lag_stats: Analyze discovery lag statistics

Health & Monitoring: - internal__kg_knowledge_health: Report access statistics — most used entries, never accessed, stale

Introspection: - introspection__get_kg_stats: Get knowledge graph statistics - introspection__search_knowledge_graph: Search for entities (DCI jobs, Jira tickets) - introspection__get_kg_entity: Get specific entity details

These work automatically during conversations.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text: Embedding exclusions (KnowledgeGraph.NON_EMBEDDED_TYPES), the dedup threshold used by compaction-time extraction (AiAssistAgent.DEDUP_SIM_THRESHOLD) and skill_performance bookkeeping are described in ARCHITECTURE § Knowledge graph.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text: The agent learns and remembers information from conversations: - Your preferences (coding style, tools, workflows) - Lessons learned (patterns, gotchas, best practices) - Project context (team info, goals, constraints) - Decision rationale (why choices were made)

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Automatic - The agent decides when to learn and save knowledge. No user action required.

You: I prefer pytest over unittest for Python testing
Agent: Got it! I'll use pytest.
      [Saves: user_preference:python_test_framework]

# Next conversation...
You: Write tests for login
Agent: I'll write pytest tests...
      [Recalled from knowledge base]

docs.text:
Just ask the agent:

ai-assist /interactive

You: What do you know about me?
You: What have you learned?
You: Show me your knowledge graph

Or run the inspector:

python examples/inspect_knowledge_base.py

docs.title: Where is it stored?
docs.text:
~/.ai-assist/knowledge_graph.db

SQLite database with bi-temporal tracking (when learned, when valid).

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Q: Does the agent save everything I say? A: Yes. All conversation exchanges are stored in the Knowledge Graph as they happen. A KG synthesis task then reviews the day's conversations and extracts structured knowledge (preferences, lessons, context, decisions).

Q: Can I delete stored knowledge? A: Yes, ask the agent to expire it ("that preference is outdated") or manually edit the SQLite database. The agent uses internal__expire_knowledge to mark entries as no longer valid or retract incorrect beliefs.

Q: How much does it store? A: Only what you explicitly state or the agent learns from conversation. Typical: 10-50 entries.

Q: Does it work offline? A: Knowledge retrieval works offline. Synthesis requires Claude API (uses Haiku model).

Q: Can I see synthesis happen? A: Synthesis runs as a nightly scheduled task (configurable in event-schedules.json). You'll see logs in monitor mode when it runs.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
1. Be explicit when stating preferences:
  2. "I prefer pytest over unittest"

  3. "I switched to neovim" (agent will expire old preference and save the new one)

  4. Ask the agent to recall:

  5. "What testing framework do I prefer?"

  6. "What have you learned about DCI?"

  7. Query by time:

  8. "What did you know yesterday at 3pm?"
  9. "What have you learned since Monday?"

  10. "What was happening on June 15?"

  11. Store future plans:

  12. "I'll be at a conference in Berlin on July 10" (stored with future valid_from)

  13. "What are my upcoming plans?" (agent searches with include_future=true)

  14. Correct the agent:

  15. "That lesson about Friday failures was wrong" (agent will retract it)

  16. "I no longer use vim" (agent will expire the preference)

  17. Check periodically what's stored:

  18. "Show me all your stored knowledge"

  19. Or run: python examples/inspect_knowledge_base.py

  20. Backup your knowledge base: 

    cp ~/.ai-assist/knowledge_graph.db ~/backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).db

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: ai-assist maintains detailed logs to help with debugging and monitoring agent behavior.

docs.title: Log Files
docs.text:
Logs are automatically written to:

~/.ai-assist/logs/ai-assist-YYYY-MM-DD.log

A new log file is created each day. For example: - ai-assist-2026-03-31.log - ai-assist-2026-04-01.log

docs.title: Log Levels
docs.text:
ai-assist uses Python's standard logging levels:

Level Description Typical Use DEBUG Detailed diagnostic information Troubleshooting, development INFO General informational messages Normal operation tracking WARNING Warning messages (non-critical issues) Potential problems ERROR Error messages (failures) Operation failures CRITICAL Critical failures Severe errors

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Logging is configured separately for file output and console output.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL - Controls what gets written to log files - Default: INFO - Values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL - Recommendation: Keep at INFO or DEBUG for comprehensive logs

AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL - Controls what appears in the terminal - Default: WARNING - Values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL - Recommendation: Keep at WARNING to avoid cluttering terminal output

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
By default (no environment variables set): - File logs: Everything at INFO level and above - Console output: Only WARNING and ERROR messages

This keeps your terminal clean while maintaining detailed logs for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Standard Operation (Default)
docs.text:
ai-assist

Result: - File: INFO, WARNING, ERROR messages - Console: WARNING, ERROR messages

docs.title: Debug Mode (Verbose)
docs.text:
export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=INFO
ai-assist

Result: - File: All messages including DEBUG - Console: INFO, WARNING, ERROR messages

docs.title: Quiet Mode (Errors Only)
docs.text:
export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR
ai-assist

Result: - File: Only ERROR and CRITICAL messages - Console: Only ERROR and CRITICAL messages

docs.title: One-Time Debug Run
docs.text:
No need to export - just set for this command:

AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG ai-assist

docs.title: Permanent Configuration
docs.text:
Add to your ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.profile:

# ai-assist logging configuration
export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=INFO
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING

docs.title: Tail Current Log
docs.text: tail -f ~/.ai-assist/logs/ai-assist-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).log

docs.title: View All Logs
docs.text: ls -lh ~/.ai-assist/logs/

docs.title: Search Logs
docs.text:
# Find all errors
grep "ERROR" ~/.ai-assist/logs/*.log

# Find specific message
grep "context overflow" ~/.ai-assist/logs/*.log

# Find messages from specific module
grep "ai_assist.agent" ~/.ai-assist/logs/*.log

docs.title: View Last 100 Lines
docs.text: tail -100 ~/.ai-assist/logs/ai-assist-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).log

docs.title: Follow Logs in Real-Time with Filtering
docs.text:
# Only show warnings and errors
tail -f ~/.ai-assist/logs/ai-assist-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).log | grep -E "WARNING|ERROR"

# Only show specific module
tail -f ~/.ai-assist/logs/ai-assist-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).log | grep "ai_assist.agent"

docs.title: Log Format
docs.text:
Each log entry contains:

TIMESTAMP - MODULE - LEVEL - MESSAGE

Example:

2026-03-31 17:15:33,456 - ai_assist.filesystem_tools - WARNING - Command 'tar' requires confirmation
2026-03-31 17:15:34,789 - ai_assist.mcp_client - ERROR - MCP server connection failed: timeout

docs.title: File Logs (Default: INFO level)
docs.text:
• Agent initialization and configuration
  • MCP server connections and disconnections
  • Tool executions and results
  • API calls and token usage
  • Knowledge graph operations
  • Scheduled action executions
  • Cache hits and misses
  • Configuration loading
  • Errors and exceptions with stack traces

docs.title: Console Output (Default: WARNING level)
docs.text:
• Warnings about potential issues
  • Error messages
  • Critical failures

Note: Normal agent output (responses, tool use notifications) is not part of logging - that goes directly to the terminal/TUI.

docs.title: No Log Files Created
docs.text:
Check that the config directory exists:

ls -la ~/.ai-assist/logs/

If it doesn't exist, ai-assist will create it on startup.

docs.title: Logs Too Verbose
docs.text:
Reduce the log level:

export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR

docs.title: Need More Detail for Debugging
docs.text:
Enable DEBUG level:

export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG

docs.title: Terminal Cluttered with Log Messages
docs.text:
The console log level is too low. Increase it:

export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING  # or ERROR

docs.title: Want Logs But Clean Terminal
docs.text:
This is the default behavior! Just use:

# File gets detailed logs, console stays clean
export AI_ASSIST_LOG_LEVEL=INFO
export AI_ASSIST_CONSOLE_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING

docs.title: Log Rotation
docs.text:
Currently, logs are not automatically rotated - each day gets a new file, but old files are kept indefinitely.

To manually clean old logs:

# Delete logs older than 30 days
find ~/.ai-assist/logs/ -name "*.log" -mtime +30 -delete

# Archive logs older than 7 days
find ~/.ai-assist/logs/ -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -exec gzip {} \;

You can add this to a cron job for automatic cleanup:

# Clean logs older than 30 days daily at 2am
0 2 * * * find ~/.ai-assist/logs/ -name "*.log" -mtime +30 -delete

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep file logging at INFO or DEBUG - disk space is cheap, missing logs are expensive
  2. Keep console logging at WARNING - reduces terminal clutter
  3. Check logs when debugging issues - they contain valuable context
  4. Use grep/tail for log analysis - don't try to read the whole file
  5. Set DEBUG mode only when troubleshooting - it generates a lot of output
